Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for South Africa's batting. The Indian players take their respective spots on the field. Aiden Markram is accompanied by Ryan Rickelton to open for the Proteas. Jasprit Bumrah has the new ball and is raring to go. Two slips and a gully await. Rickelton to face. Off we go again...
... THIRD INNINGS ...

Was the pitch too difficult to bat on? Or did the Indian batters just threw their wickets away in the process? The answer is somewhat between those. But the way Washington Sundar and Kuldeep Yadav batted for their 72-run stand for the eighth wicket, it showed that the pitch was still good enough to bat on. It was just about spending more time on the pitch with application, which the Indian middle order failed to do. Their resistance of Kuldeep and Washington lasted for 208 balls before Simon Harmer and Marco Jansen wrapped up the tail. Marco Jansen achieved his fourth Test five-wicket haul and made good use of the bounce he got. Right then, South Africa have the upper hand in this Test and they will aim to take the game far away from India's reach, which has already slipped away. Back in a bit with South Africa's reply with the bat. Stay tuned.

What's happened to India while batting at home, one wonders. They have looked uncomfortable in their own backyard. It was a steady start for India with Yashasvi Jaiswal and KL Rahul first seeing off the tricky phase late on Day 2 and then seeing off the early part of Day 3. The home side looked in a decent position at 95/1, but once Jaiswal perished, it all fell apart. First, it was Simon Harmer who dented India, and then, after the Tea break, Marco Jansen piled on the misery for the hosts. It was a procession on either side of the break as India were reduced to 122/7.

Decision-making time, then. Temba Bavuma is rushing off the field to have a chat with Shukri Conrad, their head coach, regarding the follow-on. He asks for a couple of minutes. And here's the decision. SOUTH AFRICA WILL BAT, he gestures. He has also asked for a light roller before they come out to bat again. A job well done by the Proteas. Though it took a bit longer than they would have expected, due to the resistance offered by the Indian lower order, but they still have a lead of 288 runs at their disposal and they can feel that they have both hands on the series trophy now.

The ball raps him on the gloves and balloons behind, where the keeper, Kyle Verreynne, does the rest by settling underneath it. Jansen finishes with 6 wickets. India have been bowled out for 201, falling 288 runs short of South Africa's 489.

Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for the post-Lunch session. Some last-minute instructions from Temba Bavuma in the South African huddle. Zubayr Hamza is on the field for Marco Jansen, who has not taken the field just yet. Simon Harmer will kickstart proceedings for the tourists. Kuldeep Yadav to face the first ball. A slip and a short leg await. Here we go!
... DAY 3, SESSION 3 ...

As the ball has gotten older, the bite it offered in the morning and early in the afternoon session has faded. The surface, too, has remained good for batting, with Kuldeep and Sundar showing that if you are willing to occupy the crease, the runs are there for the taking. This pair remains India’s best hope of avoiding the follow-on, with them needing another 116 runs. After a good lunch break, the South African bowlers will be raring to go again. We are yet to see Senuran Muthusamy in this innings, and his introduction may not be far away. The second new ball is still 13 overs away, and if India get that far, South Africa will, in all likelihood, take it straightaway and look to finish the job. After the wobble before Tea, India would have hoped for some stability at the start of the afternoon session, but it turned out to be anything but that. Rishabh Pant left much to be desired with the shot selection and the timing of it, and what followed was further capitulation as Marco Jansen used the short ball to good effect. From being 95/1 at one stage, the hosts collapsed spectacularly to be reduced to 122/7. Washington Sundar and Kuldeep Yadav arrested the slide and as the session wore on, the pair grew in confidence.

Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for the post-Tea session. The two umpires and players make their way out to the centre. South Africa are starting with spin in the form of Simon Harmer. Rishabh Pant to face. A slip and a backward short leg in place. Let's go...
... DAY 3, SESSION 2 ...

Jaiswal cruised to a well-crafted fifty, looking in complete control. Sai Sudharsan came in looking scratchy at first, but gradually found his feet. The two lefties were starting to put together a partnership that was nicely blossoming. But then Harmer struck a hammer-blow twice in no time and fished out both Jaiswal and Sudharsan. And with Jurel getting out on a rash shot, failing to read the slowness of the pitch, India slipped down from 95/1 to 102/4. With two new batters at the crease and a couple more proper batters left to come, India have their back against the wall at the moment. Though they are still 188 runs adrift to avoid a follow-on, the Proteas will aim to dent this middle order as quickly as they come back for the afternoon session. As of now, the South Africans hold all the aces, and India are walking a tight rope. Play resumes at 11.20 am IST (5.50 am GMT). Join us then.

Then the spinners entered the chat and everything changed. On a pitch that was already gripping and turning, Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer immediately dialed into the perfect frequency. They tossed it up beautifully, giving the ball proper air time between 75 and 85 clicks. Nothing flat or rushed about it. The ball was landing, biting, and asking serious questions every single delivery. Jaiswal, however, kept milking runs with his sweeps, but just before the drinks break, KL Rahul's resistance crumbled and South Africa had their opening.

The morning session crawled along and was a slow-burn when the quicks had the ball. Sure, there was a bit of movement here and there, but nothing that made the Indian openers lose sleep. They settled in nicely, content to nudge and rotate without taking silly risks through that opening spell. Jaiswal found his groove first and started putting away the bad balls with authority, while KL Rahul kept his head down and played the anchor role. The partnership was ticking along smoothly as the two added 56 runs to their overnight score in the first hour.

South Africa's session hands down. They have run through the top order of India in the last half an hour or so and are well and truly bossing this game now. India were looking good with KL Rahul and Jaiswal settling in nicely in the first hour, but the second hour belonged to the visitors. The spinners disrupted the momentum and found good purchase off the deck as well. With this, South Africa have now won six sessions out of seven played in this second Test. India, on the other hand, have a lot of catching up to do.

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK! With the wicket of KL Rahul, South Africa end the first hour on a high. It was turning out to be a good start to the day for India until then. Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj have been quick to assess the correct pace to bowl on this surface and varied their speeds, something Indian spinners did not do. From India's perspective, Yashasvi Jaiswal holds the key here in not letting the spinners settle. Temba Bavuma has been smart with setting in out fields, knowing that it is the home side that has to make the move and they have to take their chances. Sai Sudharsan is in at number 3.

OUT! EDGED AND TAKEN! Finally, the resistance is broken by Maharaj. Keshav drops it full and gets a bit of drift into the batter, well under 80 kph. It lands and then sharply spins away from the right-hander with some bounce. KL Rahul is drawn forward and pushes at the delivery, goes with hard hands and gets a thick outside edge. The ball goes to the right of the first slip fielder, where Aiden Markram gets low and gathers a fine catch in his safe hands. KL Rahul is disappointed as he walks back for 22 (63). India are 65/1, trailing by 424 runs.

PITCH REPORT - Deep Dasgupta and Shaun Pollock are inspecting the third day's pitch of Guwahati. Deep first informs that it is a nippy, overcast morning. Pollock joins him and says it still looks like a decent batting pitch. Also adds that the pace of the pitch has slowed down as well, and expects it to continue to do so as the game progresses. Observes very minimal wear and tear, but nothing serious. Deep further adds that the wear and tear will increase, but also thinks that there are not many demons as yet. Pollock then details by saying that the footmarks have started to get more and more prominent. Stresses that the batters must apply themselves to get big runs, as he reckons that different bowlers are going to create different chances from this track.

What South Africa’s batting effort has also done is take significant time out of the game, with the visitors nearly batting across six sessions. With India trailing in the series, they will need to make the running from here. All eyes will be on their intent with the bat and on whether the pitch, which has so far been good for batting, begins to show any signs of deterioration as the day progresses. It is all set up for an intriguing day. Stick around.

Before we look ahead, a quick recap of Day 2. South Africa resumed on 246/6 and marched their way to 489, thanks largely to Senuran Muthusamy’s maiden Test hundred and Marco Jansen’s superb 93. It was a frustrating Sunday for India, who were made to toil long and hard. In reply, Yashasvi Jaiswal and KL Rahul had a tricky period to negotiate in fading light but managed to get through unscathed.

Hello and a warm welcome, folks! While the opening day in Guwahati ended on a fairly even footing, Day 2 belonged entirely to South Africa. What does Day 3 have in store for us? You get the feeling that if India are to harbour any realistic chance of winning this Test, today becomes their make-or-break day. A strong performance will keep them in the hunt, but if things drift the other way, this contest might slip out of their reach by the end of this all-important ‘Moving Day’.

So, India are trailing in the series and their tired minds need to freshen up as they have to force an issue to level it up. Still three days remaining, but the Proteas have put themselves in a very comfortable position and can dictate the terms from here on. It's a good batting wicket, but as we head to the 'Moving Day', expect the Proteas spinners to come into play as well. Join us for the action of Day 3 at 9 am IST (3.30 am GMT). Till then, cheers!

Senuran Muthusamy is in for a chat. He says it is a special moment for him to score his maiden Test ton and he is glad to have contributed in the first innings, knowing how important those runs always are. Shares that the focus was on building partnerships, extending the innings, and scoring wherever possible. He praises Kyle Verreynne for batting well and calls Marco Jansen's knock special. Adds that he had the best seat in the house to watch Marco’s ball-striking. On the DRS incident where he managed to overturn after being given LBW, he admits he felt there might have been a brush of the glove, but the emotions of getting out meant it did not fully register in the moment. He concludes by saying they will wait and see how the pitch plays.

The Guwahati crowd got their voice back when Kyle Verreynne fell to a reckless drive but they were silenced quickly by the incoming Marco Jansen, who came in with wings in his levers. Jansen not only kept the crowd quiet but sucked out energy from the Indian players by scoring at the rate of knots. His innings proved to be the turning point for South Africa as his lone effort helped them get close to 500. On the other hand, India toiled hard with the ball. Bowling 151.1 overs, Rishabh Pant had no option but to throw the ball to the seamers as Marco Jansen was taking on the spinners pretty easily. Kuldeep Yadav was the pick of the lot as he ended with a four-fer.

Reeling at 246/6, Senuran Muthusamy and Kyle Verreynne showed character and application in the morning session to build a base to play on. Once the Indian bowlers got a bit inconsistent, South Africa jumped onto the scene by scoring runs. Both batters took their time to dwell in, but once they applied themselves, it was a long grind for the hosts.

So, a bumpy period for India to bat after fielding throughout the day. Just the 6.1 overs they had to negotiate and the openers did the job. What a day for South Africa. It thoroughly belongs to them. What a fightback they have shown. From Markram to Maharaj, everyone chipped in with runs. They were coming today under some pressure. They were 246/6 with India's tail up in the morning but South Africa's lower order managed to add 243 runs, with Senuran Muthusamy highlighting the batting package.
